records.name: Irrigation Works
records.description: Unmanned water-control infrastructure that grants irrigated plots to agricultural holdings. Higher tiers may be built directly when the settlement has the technology, labor, and materials to support them.

serviceOutputs.description: Provides irrigated plot access to farming workplaces.

constructionPolicy.notes: Upgrading older works costs more labor than direct construction because channels, retaining structures, and grades must be partially dismantled and rebuilt while water flow is rerouted.

benefits: Supports small gardens and hand-watered plots near springs and deep aquifers.
Works without a large civic water network but serves only a narrow footprint.
tiers.buildNotes: Best suited to early holdings where irrigation is local and manually lifted.

benefits: Stabilizes ordinary field irrigation from rivers, lakes, and springs.
Enables broader crop rotation but requires ongoing channel clearing and embankment repair.
tiers.buildNotes: Best for common farmsteads and valley plots with easy surface-water access.

benefits: Improves reliability and lets settlements bridge more complicated channel corridors.
Pairs well with managed farmsteads that need steadier flow and cleaner routing.
tiers.buildNotes: Wood lining reduces seepage but raises material and carpentry demand.

benefits: Feeds larger orchards and terraced plots with gated, stone-supported flow.
Integrates cleanly with more permanent civic construction and hillside routing.
tiers.buildNotes: Valve control and stonework sharply increase both up-front labor and material quality requirements.

benefits: Supports long-range water movement, estate-scale agriculture, and civic prestige projects.
Can feed distant plots directly instead of relying only on local branch channels.
tiers.buildNotes: Best built directly when a settlement can afford it; retrofitting to this scale is intentionally labor-heavy.

records.name: Road Network
records.description: Unmanned overland transport infrastructure that improves hauling, travel reliability, and market linkage across a settlement's lanes and arteries.

serviceOutputs.description: Provides dependable overland route access for hauling and travel.
Supports heavier wagon and pack-train movement along maintained corridors.

constructionPolicy.notes: Refitting an old lane into a better road costs more labor than laying a new segment because grading, resurfacing, drainage correction, and traffic rerouting all add extra work.

benefits: Establishes recognizable travel lanes between homes, stores, and nearby worksites.
Reduces total travel waste for very small settlements and camps.
tiers.buildNotes: A low-cost starting point for settlements that have not yet committed to engineered roads.

benefits: Supports regular hauling between extraction sites, mills, and markets.
Improves route legibility for teamsters and procurement traffic.
tiers.buildNotes: Usually the first road tier worth laying deliberately for commerce instead of simple travel.

benefits: Keeps heavy loads moving through softer ground and wet approaches.
Lets larger settlements maintain dependable haul corridors across rougher terrain.
tiers.buildNotes: Best for muddy approaches, marsh edges, and busy roads before full stone surfacing is affordable.

benefits: Greatly improves reliability for market throughput and military movement.
Supports denser districts without roads collapsing into mud cycles.
tiers.buildNotes: A large jump in labor because drainage, grading, and stone setting all matter at once.

benefits: Turns major corridors into all-season trade routes with stable hauling capacity.
Supports larger market density, administrative reach, and rapid district movement.
tiers.buildNotes: Best built fresh when a settlement is already dense enough to justify a true civic arterial network.

records.name: Bridgeworks
records.description: Permanent crossing infrastructure that links roads over streams, rivers, gorges, and later navigable canals without requiring continuous ferry labor.

serviceOutputs.description: Provides a fixed crossing point for roads, caravans, and civilian traffic.

constructionPolicy.notes: Bridge retrofits are labor-hungry because old supports must be shored, removed, and replaced while the crossing remains partially usable or fully rerouted.

benefits: Removes the need to ford minor waterways on foot routes.
Keeps seasonal travel interruptions from fully isolating nearby districts.
tiers.buildNotes: A practical first crossing, but too fragile for sustained wagon traffic.

benefits: Connects ordinary road traffic across rivers without constant ferry handling.
Supports early trade routes and routine wagon movement.
tiers.buildNotes: A strong upgrade for settlements that need regular but not monumental crossings.

benefits: Provides a durable crossing for heavy commerce and organized defense response.
Reduces flood disruption compared with purely timber-supported spans.
Supports clear spans and foundations suitable for engineered canal crossings.
tiers.buildNotes: A major commitment in stone and masonry, but far more resilient over time.

benefits: Creates a monumental crossing for heavily used commercial and military routes.
Serves as a reliable overpass for major river and canal traffic corridors.
Pairs well with advanced road and canal infrastructure at city scale.
tiers.buildNotes: Usually justified only for important arterial routes or prestigious urban crossings.

records.name: Defensive Walls
records.description: Static perimeter defenses that shape access, absorb raids, and project settlement strength without requiring a permanently staffed workplace model.

serviceOutputs.description: Provides a defended perimeter that gates, towers, and patrol systems can build upon.

constructionPolicy.notes: Wall retrofits are expensive because older lines must be dismantled, foundations widened, and temporary breaches secured while stronger works are raised.

benefits: Creates a clear boundary and slows opportunistic raiders or wild animals.
Helps channel movement toward watched entry points.
tiers.buildNotes: Fast to erect, but vulnerable to weathering and fire.

benefits: Provides a more forgiving and resilient defensive line than simple palisades.
Improves survivability of frontier towns and estates.
tiers.buildNotes: Labor-intensive because the earth itself becomes the fortification.

benefits: Marks the settlement as a serious fortified center rather than a temporary enclosure.
Works cleanly with more advanced gates, towers, and patrol routes.
tiers.buildNotes: A large leap in stone demand, but it establishes a durable urban perimeter.

benefits: Adds observation and layered defense to the perimeter without needing a separate workplace type.
Supports larger towns, citadels, and contested border settlements.
tiers.buildNotes: Much heavier foundation work than simple wall thickening because towers change load paths.

benefits: Turns the perimeter into a major civic work with defensive, symbolic, and administrative value.
Best supports large urban centers, citadels, and capitals.
tiers.buildNotes: Usually better to build new planned sections than retrofit cramped older walls into this scale.

records.name: Civic Aqueducts
records.description: Long-span civic water conveyance infrastructure for moving clean water into dense districts, baths, workshops, and future utility networks without modeling it as a staffed workplace.

serviceOutputs.description: Provides engineered long-range water routing for irrigation and civic distribution.
Represents stable high-volume water service inside dense districts.

constructionPolicy.notes: Aqueduct retrofits are unusually expensive because arches, channels, settling basins, and urban delivery lines must be dismantled and rebuilt without collapsing water service entirely.

benefits: Provides the first engineered civic water line beyond simple local lifting.
Can feed nearby workshops, bath sites, and irrigated districts.
tiers.buildNotes: Useful where terrain already favors a clean downhill grade.

benefits: Improves cleanliness and reliability for denser neighborhoods and bath culture.
Supports more than one major consumer without constant manual intervention.
tiers.buildNotes: Usually the first tier that feels like a true civic water project instead of a clever ditch.

benefits: Extends water service across uneven ground without depending on local wells at every district.
Creates the backbone needed for large irrigation and civic water projects.
tiers.buildNotes: The point where aqueducts start shaping settlement form rather than merely supporting it.

benefits: Carries water across more difficult terrain and denser settlement footprints.
Supports larger baths, fountains, workshops, and irrigated outskirts.
tiers.buildNotes: A technical leap that rewards already-large settlements with far stronger water reach.

benefits: Provides the backbone for a large city's civic water culture and future utility layers.
Pairs cleanly with irrigation networks, baths, fountains, and dense urban production.
tiers.buildNotes: A prestige-scale project that is usually easier to build planned sections of directly than to retrofit from patchwork older lines.

records.name: Gate Systems
records.description: Static entry-control infrastructure for walled settlements, controlling traffic, chokepoints, and defensible access without being treated as a staffed workplace.

serviceOutputs.description: Provides controlled entry points that pair with roads and defensive walls.

constructionPolicy.notes: Gate upgrades require dismantling doors, lintels, and control hardware while maintaining or temporarily rerouting secure access through the wall line.

benefits: Creates a controllable entry instead of an open gap in the perimeter.
Gives even simple walls a meaningful checkpoint and closure point.
tiers.buildNotes: Enough for small towns and palisades, but not ideal for constant heavy use.

benefits: Handles heavier routine traffic while still closing reliably under stress.
Improves choke-point control on busier roads and market entries.
tiers.buildNotes: A practical balance between throughput and defensibility.

benefits: Turns entrances into serious defensive structures rather than oversized doors.
Works well with stronger walls and more formal urban traffic control.
tiers.buildNotes: The first truly urban gate tier, with enough mass and mechanism to matter in siege conditions.

benefits: Balances urban traffic throughput with prestige and layered security.
Best supports major capitals, market towns, and citadel districts.
tiers.buildNotes: A major gateway project that functions as both civic statement and defensive apparatus.

records.name: Canal Network
records.description: Engineered inland waterways that carry boats, barges, and cargo traffic across otherwise non-navigable land routes.

serviceOutputs.description: Provides an inland navigable water route for shallow-draft transport and ship support infrastructure.

constructionPolicy.notes: Canal retrofits are more labor-intensive than direct construction because embankments, sluices, towpaths, and partial water control have to be rebuilt while old channels are drained or diverted.

benefits: Opens the first practical inland water shortcut for hand-hauled or poled craft.
Pairs well with nearby storehouses before heavier trade infrastructure exists.
tiers.buildNotes: A starter navigation channel that is cheap to field but shallow and maintenance-hungry.

benefits: Carries routine freight more reliably than open earth cuts and flood ditches.
Improves waterborne movement between farms, mills, and river markets.
tiers.buildNotes: The first tier that behaves like a proper working freight canal instead of a local shortcut.

benefits: Supports heavier cargo boats and more reliable water levels through engineered banks.
Creates a believable civic-scale navigation route rather than a rural works cut.
tiers.buildNotes: A major jump in durability and carrying capacity for inland navigation.

benefits: Moves boats across elevation changes that would stop lower canal tiers entirely.
Adds the first true lock infrastructure and serious repair support for working barges.
tiers.buildNotes: This is the tier where canals stop being local transport aids and become regional infrastructure.

benefits: Supports high-volume inland shipping and ship servicing far from natural deepwater routes.
Combines locks, basins, and drydock capacity into a true engineered water-transport corridor.
tiers.buildNotes: A prestige-scale civil works project that is usually planned as a fresh build rather than retrofitted from older canal cuts.
